name: Profit Margin (Activity-Based Costing)
description: Recompute profit margin once overhead is allocated by activity instead of a single blanket rate.
formula: Net Profit = Revenue − COGS − Operating Expenses; Margin % = Net Profit / Revenue. At advanced difficulty, Operating Expenses is replaced by activity-based overhead: Total Overhead = (Setup Driver Qty × Setup Rate) + (Inspection Driver Qty × Inspection Rate); Net Profit = Revenue − COGS − Total Overhead.
business_contexts: a specialty grocer comparing how much of every dollar of sales it actually keeps
a contract manufacturer reviewing how much of its sales survive after costs
an online retailer reviewing how much of each sales dollar survives after costs
a franchise reviewing how much of its sales it keeps after expenses
a precision parts manufacturer recomputing margin after switching to activity-based costing for its production overhead
question_patterns: Of every dollar the client brings in, what share is actually kept after costs?
What percentage of the client's sales survives once costs are subtracted?
What is the margin once overhead is allocated by activity instead of one blanket rate?
How does the margin change when setup and inspection costs are traced to what actually drives them?
solution_logic: Step 1: Calculate net profit = revenue − cogs − operating_expenses
Step 2: Calculate margin = net profit / revenue
Step 1 (advanced): Calculate setup overhead = setup_driver_qty × setup_rate
Step 2 (advanced): Calculate inspection overhead = inspection_driver_qty × inspection_rate
Step 3 (advanced): Calculate total overhead = setup overhead + inspection overhead
Step 4 (advanced): Calculate net profit = revenue − cogs − total overhead
Step 5 (advanced): Calculate margin = net profit / revenue
key_insight: A single blanket overhead rate can hide which activities actually drive cost — activity-based costing traces overhead to what causes it, and that can move the margin meaningfully.
common_mistakes: Dividing by cost instead of revenue
Adding operating expenses AND activity-based overhead instead of replacing one with the other
Treating the driver quantity alone as the cost, instead of multiplying it by its rate
framework_soundbite: Profit margin is profit over revenue — and profit is only as accurate as how honestly you've traced overhead to what actually drives it.
